en: The Sūtra on Right Reverence, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

He was accompanied by two hundred and fifty śrāvaka bhikṣus and five hundred bodhisattvas—all of whom were seeds of the Tathāgata, who practice expediently within the six realms to assist the Buddha in spreading his transformation, who know the faculties of sentient beings and possess sovereign majestic virtue, and who manifest the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means—whose names were: Bodhisattva Susaṃśaya... [and so forth].
Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva, Prabhāpāla Bodhisattva, Prajñottara Bodhisattva,
Guṇasamudgata Bodhisattva, Siddhārtha Bodhisattva, Abhaya Bodhisattva, Bodhimukha Bodhisattva, Dhanamukha Bodhisattva,
Ratnamukha Bodhisattva, Guṇamukha Bodhisattva, Netramukha Bodhisattva, and Vīryamukha Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Dharmottara, the Bodhisattva Prajñottara, the Bodhisattva Bhadrottara,
and five hundred such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were present together with him.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How should sons and daughters of good family who delight in the Dharma revere the Dharma and revere the Dharma teacher?"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Stop, stop, Ānanda!
"At this time, sentient beings are unable to show respect or possess the dharma of respect.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"I now delight in the Dharma and revere the Dharma; I have revered it and shall continue to revere it.
World-Honored One!
Since I first drew near to the Tathāgata, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate."
Because we have not heard [this teaching], we would surely lose our proper decorum in showing reverence to the Tathāgata.
Now that we have heard it, we shall be able to practice this matter in accordance with the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who delight in the Dharma and, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, immediately attain its practice.
World-Honored One!

There are also bhikṣus who have gone forth within the Tathāgata’s Dharma, yet who are poor and lowly, seeking only food and clothing, and taking no pleasure in seeking the Dharma or honoring the Dharma masters.
"Although we may draw near to the Buddha-dharma, we act in a base and lowly manner and cannot conceal it; it must inevitably be manifested.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, I now, on behalf of myself and all bhikṣus of the future, respectfully request the Tathāgata for such a teaching."
“World-Honored One!
How should we cultivate correct practice?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for us.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a son or daughter of good family who delights in and reveres the Dharma wishes to read, recite, or inquire about it, they should go to where the sūtras and teachings are kept, to their upādhyāya or ācārya."
Having arrived at their location, one should inquire of the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the ācārya regarding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata according to what one’s own mind desires.
One should understand that regarding the dharmas known in the minds of the preceptor and the ācārya, one must first consult them and ask whether or not one may listen to and inquire about them.
If the teacher consents, only then should one ask questions.
Even if one is only ten or twenty years of age, for the sake of delighting in the Dharma, one should go to consult him and receive his formal reliance (*niśraya*).

Why is this? Although within the Dharma of the Tathāgata it is permitted for a bhikṣu of five years' standing to be free from dependence on a preceptor, such a person nevertheless maintains initial reverence because they seek the Dharma.
Why is this? Because this person desires to accomplish their own virtuous conduct. Ānanda!
That ācārya should grant the dependence in this manner, either saying:
"It may be so," or saying: [the other phrase].
"Yes," he replied, or said, "So it is."
Some said: "It is beneficial.
Others said: [it is not].
"Exhortation":
some say, "Act with vigilance and do not be negligent; practice correctly and uprightly in accordance with the Dharma."

"Having granted the formal authorization (*niśraya*) in this manner, if a bhikṣu is endowed with such qualities as these, he may be granted the authorization; he is then said to be one who has successfully accomplished the authorization."

If even a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing cannot penetrate such phrases as these, that person should receive dependence [from others]; how much less could he act as a teacher of dependence for others?
If a bhikṣu of even one year's standing accomplishes such dharmas as these, his secret words as a śramaṇa shall be recognized as having received formal reliance (*niśraya*).
Conversely, even if he has been ordained for a hundred years, if he does not personally master such phrases and rules of the Vinaya, he must receive formal reliance.
Among these, a bhikṣu who recites the sūtras should maintain a mind of profound respect toward his ācārya, as well as proper reverence for those who read, recite, or receive the sūtras from him.

In the presence of the ācārya, he must not show his teeth, gaze at the teacher’s feet, move his feet, stack his feet, cross his legs, or fidget with his feet. He must not sit on a seat higher than the teacher's; unless the teacher asks a question, he must not speak, nor should he disobey the teacher’s words, nor gaze fixedly at the teacher’s face.
Standing three cubits before the teacher, one sits when the teacher permits sitting; having sat down, one should arouse a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward the teacher.
The reciter should first master the scripture through thorough rehearsal; once it is mastered, they may receive the scripture from the teacher in whatever amount they wish.
If there are any doubts regarding any of the Dharma-gates, one should first inquire whether it is permissible to ask questions.
If the teacher grants permission, one may then question him.
Having received the scripture, one should place the right knee on the ground and join both hands to pay homage at the teacher’s feet.
If the ground is uneven, one should retreat along whatever path leads back until reaching level ground.
If the ground is already level, one should pay homage at the feet of the teacher before proceeding.
When they have walked ten cubits, they should again prostrate and then proceed along the path.
They should form this thought:
"The ācārya always follows behind me; I cannot distance myself from the ācārya."
He should know the proper time and go to the ācārya’s place three times each day.
If he does not go, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If he arrives but does not see the ācārya, he should leave a mark using grass, wood, a staff, a clod of earth, or a stone.
If the ācārya is sitting in retreat within his room, one should circumambulate the room to pay respects before proceeding.
If there is anything to be done, one must not act without asking the teacher, except for the acts of defecation and urination.
One must not address the teacher with coarse, vulgar, or evil speech, nor should one repeat the teacher’s words verbatim.
Wherever the teacher sits—whether on a corded seat or a wooden bench—one must not sit there oneself.
If that bed should break, it must be repaired immediately.
One should go there at dawn and go at the appropriate time; one must not go there at an inappropriate time.
Having arrived, one should ask the ācārya:
"What do you require, and what must be done?
Will you enter the village?

If he says he will enter, the preceptor should wash his hands and wipe them with his own robes; having grasped the teacher's robe with both hands, he should place it in a clean spot. First, he gives the teacher pure water for washing the hands, and then he presents the robe to the teacher. Afterward, he dusts the *antarvāsa* (inner robe) and gives it to him, or [presents] the upper garment (*saṃkakṣikā*) or the rain cloak (*varṣāśāṭī*).
Or those who require other robes and requisites.

He should show such respect that he must not sneeze or spit in the presence of the ācārya; whether inside the monastery or in its eastern or western quarters, he must not fold his robe over both shoulders or wrap it around his head while following his teacher to his dwelling place.

He swept and sprinkled the walking path to make it clean; he fanned [the teacher] three times a day, bathed him three times a day, and three times a day he inquired after his needs, fetched water, and went out to beg for food on behalf of his teacher.
If the teacher has something to do, the student should apply himself with effort to perform it.
When the meal is finished, he should ask the teacher for his bowl to wash it.
If the teacher gives it to him, he should first wash the teacher’s bowl and then wash his own.
If the teacher does not grant it, one must not seek it again.
Why is this? Ānanda!
In the future, there will be such bhikṣus who will think to themselves:
"The bowl of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has no one to wash it.
Because they wish to emulate me, they will desire to wash it themselves.
The Tathāgata permits such persons as these to take coolness in summer and warmth in winter; whatever they require, they should be allowed to obtain.
One must not chew a tooth-stick in the presence of one's teacher, nor speak of the teacher’s good or bad qualities. If one sees the teacher from afar, one should rise to greet him.
Ānanda! If one receives even a single four-line verse through reading, reciting, or requesting instruction, that person is called an ācārya.
For this reason, one should pay respect to the ācārya.
Ānanda! If one does not revere the ācārya in this manner, then because of that lack of reverence, one dwells in improper conduct.
One who speaks of the teacher’s faults and evils does not speak of me as the World-Honored One.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Such a person does not revere the Buddha, does not respect the Dharma, and is not counted among the Saṃgha.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Such a deluded person cannot be said to abide in right practice.
"Ānanda! It is for those who abide in right practice that I preach the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda wept and shed tears, speaking these words:
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings in future ages who are able to abide in and practice such deeds as these, they will be most rare indeed.
World-Honored One!”
"I am able to practice and abide in such conduct as this,
World-Honored One!
If there is a bhikṣu who cannot show reverence to his preceptor (upādhyāya), his ācārya, or those who point out his faults, what kind of retribution will that person receive?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there is a bhikṣu who does not respect his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), and who speaks ill of them, I declare that person to be a foolish worldling."
Why is this? Ānanda!
One must not say that an ācārya is actually evil, much less say so falsely!
In this regard, Ānanda!
If one does not show reverence toward one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), there is a hell named Ucchedana (Extinction).
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in that hell; once born there, they immediately possess four heads, and their bodies are ablaze with fire like glowing red-hot iron balls.
Within this place there are various worms called "iron dogs" that constantly devour the tongue-roots of those people.
When their lives end in this place, they are reborn among the animals as tigers, wolves, or jackals; whenever sentient beings see them, they all cry out:
"This is a tiger, a wolf, or a jackal!"
Those who have such views are unable to find joy;
because of their past verbal transgressions, they constantly consume filth and excrement.
Once their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn among humans, but always in remote borderlands where the Buddha-dharma does not exist.

Although born among humans, they are endowed with manifold evils and far removed from merit; their physical form, color, and strength do not resemble those of ordinary humans, and the body they have received does not resemble that of their parents, such that they are not cherished or loved by them.
They will constantly suffer malicious slander and remain far removed from all Buddhas; in every birth they will be foolish, dull-witted, and lacking in wisdom, quickly falling into hell. Why is this?
Because they did not respect those who taught and bestowed the Dharma, nor did they rescue those in distress.
Ānanda! Such persons as these shall experience the nature of suffering. Ānanda!

Suppose one were to read, recite, receive, and uphold even a single four-line verse, or write out a sutra scroll and make offerings to it; for as many eons as there are syllables in that text, one might carry that teacher upon one's head, shoulders, or back, and provide him with all manner of articles of pleasure as an offering.
"Ānanda! Even after making such offerings as these, one still cannot repay the kindness of the ācārya.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In future ages there will be such evil bhikṣus who, having obtained this sutra, do not show reverence toward their ācāryas and upādhyāyas; because they lack proper conduct, they will speak of the faults of their ācāryas and upādhyāyas.”
I shall now declare that such foolish bhikṣus as these will fall into the various hells and undergo great suffering and affliction.

Ānanda! I now inform you and issue this formal command: the Tathāgata has explained the conduct of the paths of good and evil; according to the good or evil deeds performed by those sentient beings, they shall receive such retribution.
Therefore, Ānanda!
You and the others should now pay proper respect and reflect with careful deliberation. Ānanda!

Good sons and good daughters who respectfully honor this Dharma-gate and attain it will praise renunciation and censure the impurity of desire; with all dust and defilements exhausted, they shall attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes once more and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What should this essential Dharma be called as a sutra?"

How should bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās receive, uphold, and practice [this teaching] so that in future ages they may succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem and ensure it is not severed?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This sutra is named ‘Right Reverence’; you should receive and uphold it in this way, which is to say: loving the Buddha, loving the Dharma, and loving the Saṅgha.”

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the bhikṣus, and all the bodhisattvas, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly elated; with joy, they reverently practiced it.
The Sutra on Right Reverence Spoken by the Buddha
